title: Why sustainable protein transitions stall: the role of consumer attitudes in constraining plant-based meat adoption in South Africa
abstract: Purpose This study examines the dominant consumer attitudes limiting the sustained and frequent consumption of plant-based meat alternatives (PBMAs), specifically plant-based burger patties, among South African consumers. While prior research has focused on reducing barriers to initial trial, persistent psychological factors continue to constrain mainstream dietary integration. The study aims to identify these attitudinal barriers and assess their relative influence on regular consumption behaviour. Design/methodology/approach The study employs principal component analysis to identify and evaluate the dominant consumer attitudes, and regression analysis was used to determine their influence on PBMA consumption. Survey data from South African consumers were analysed to determine the extent to which specific psychological constructs predict reduced frequency of plant-based burger consumption. Demographic patterns associated with these attitudes were also examined. Findings Food technology neophobia and the belief that government, rather than individuals, should drive progressiveness in the food system emerged as the dominant psychological barriers to regular PBMA consumption. Consistent with global sustainable consumption trends, these attitudes significantly reduced mainstream adoption. These barriers were less pronounced among younger consumers, females, vegans/vegetarians and individuals with higher education levels. In contrast to the mixed findings reported in previous studies, this study found that higher-income consumers exhibited stronger psychological barriers to frequent PBMA consumption, highlighting the need to better understand the income effect on PBMA consumption. Originality/value The study advances existing literature by shifting focus from trial behaviour to sustained consumption, highlighting the role of responsibility attribution and technology-related scepticism in shaping dietary transitions. It provides actionable insights for policymakers and industry stakeholders seeking to accelerate the mainstreaming of PBMAs through consumer education and targeted market strategies.

When turbulence accelerates change: technological readiness and business process reconfiguration in service firms
abstract: Purpose This study investigates the extent to which service firms exhibit technological readiness across different functional areas under conditions of heightened environmental turbulence. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities perspective, it further examines how function-level technological readiness is associated with changes in organisational processes and key resource categories. Design/methodology/approach A conceptual framework integrating environmental turbulence, dynamic capabilities, innovation, and technological readiness was developed based on review of the relevant literature. Empirical data were collected through a survey of 307 managers representing service firms. The proposed relationships were examined using multivariate regression analyses. Findings The findings indicate substantial technology-related adaptation among service firms operating during a period of heightened macroeconomic and technological turbulence, while technological readiness varies considerably across functional areas. Readiness is most strongly developed in customer- and market- oriented functions, whereas changes are particularly visible in coordination- and information-intensive processes. The results further reveal that the relationships between function-level technological readiness and organisational change are configuration-specific, exhibiting both positive and negative associations depending on the process or resource considered. These findings suggest that technological readiness does not operate as a uniformly beneficial organisational attribute but rather as a context-dependent mechanism of adaptation. Practical implications Managers should recognise that technological readiness requires cross-functional alignment and coordination to support effective organisational transformation. Investments in technological development should therefore be accompanied by efforts to ensure consistency across functional areas, processes, and resource configurations. Originality/value This study extends the literature on environmental turbulence and dynamic capabilities by introducing a function-level perspective on technological readiness. It demonstrates that readiness for technological change constitutes a micro-foundational capability whose association with organisational transformation depends on the configuration of functional areas, processes, and resources. By moving beyond firm-level analyses, the study provides new insights into how service firms adapt to turbulent environments.

title: Trend Analysis and Prediction of Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) Change in General Santos City
journal: Research Frontiers: International Journal of Social Science and Technology
abstract: This study analyzed land use and land cover (LULC) changes in General Santos City and predicted possible future LULC patterns for 2043 and 2063. It quantified changes in six LULC classes from 2003 to 2063 using a quantitative geospatial modeling approach. Landsat Imagery was the primary dataset, while validation points from historical imagery and spatial drivers, including aspect, elevation, slope, and distance to roads and rivers, were incorporated into the model. LULC maps were generated through supervised classification and validated through accuracy assessment before being used in the CA-ANN simulation. The results showed acceptable performance, with overall accuracies above 70%. Model validation also produced substantial agreement, with a Kappa coefficient of 0.67038. The results showed significant changes in LULC. Barren/Open Land decreased substantially from 5,000.20 hectares in 2003 to 1,125.98 hectares in 2023. Under a business-as-usual scenario, Built-Up areas were projected to increase from 6,045.79 hectares in 2023 to 10,075.55 hectares in 2063, while Grassland/Shrubland was projected to decline by 6,727.94 hectares. These findings emphasized continued urban expansion and conversion of transitional LULC classification into more intensive uses. The study provided spatial evidence to support sustainable urban development, land use planning, and policy formulation in General Santos City.

title: Too much pressure? The conditional impact of responsible leadership on radical creativity via job crafting
abstract: Purpose In resource-pressured manufacturing contexts, frontline employees are increasingly expected to generate radical ideas under uncertainty and work pressure. This study examines whether responsible leadership, as a source of ethical guidance, stakeholder-oriented support and work meaning, fosters employees' radical creativity in settings marked by production disruptions and operational pressure. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, this research develops a moderated mediation model in which job crafting serves as a resource conversion mechanism and challenge stressors serve as a boundary condition. The hypotheses were tested through regression analysis and bootstrap analysis based on 318 matched supervisor-subordinate dyads from seven Chinese manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises facing supply-chain instability, logistics restrictions, fluctuating orders and operational pressure. Findings Responsible leadership was positively related to employee radical creativity, both directly and indirectly through job crafting. Challenge stressors weakened the link between responsible leadership and job crafting and, consequently, the indirect effect on radical creativity. Originality/value This study shows how responsible leadership supports frontline employees' radical creativity. The findings inform leadership development and organizational practices that promote innovation without compromising employee well-being, decent work, or responsible organizational governance.

title: The Pro-Israel Lobby and Christian Zionism in the United States: Organizational Structure, Doctrinal Foundations, and Instruments of Influence on U.S. Foreign Policy toward the Middle East
journal: International Journal of Law Research and Studies
abstract: This study examines the role of the pro-Israel lobby in the United States, in both its organized Jewish and Christian Zionist components, in shaping U.S. foreign policy decisions toward the Middle East. It proceeds from the hypothesis that the lobby's effectiveness cannot be explained by its organizational and financial capacities alone, but rather by the convergence of these capacities with a broad doctrinal base within American evangelicalism, which grants it an electoral reach and cultural legitimacy that other interest groups rarely possess. Using a descriptive-analytical approach, the study draws on interest-group theory and the "ethnic lobby" thesis as an explanatory framework, and applies the case-study method to three cases: the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the 2018 relocation of the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem, and U.S. arms supply and diplomatic protection for Israel during the Gaza war (2023-2025). It concludes that the lobby's influence peaks when its objectives coincide with the orientation of the incumbent administration and the religious sentiment of its electoral base, and declines relatively when it collides with strategic priorities the administration deems more costly. The Gaza case further reveals a notable paradox: a continued flow of weapons and diplomatic cover at the decision-making level, alongside an erosion of the bipartisan consensus on Israel within the Democratic base.

title: The Effect of Green Human Resource Management Through Competitive Advantage on the Performance of Culinary Msmes in Bogor City
journal: Neo Journal of economy and social humanities
abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) on Competitive Advantage and MSME Performance, as well as the effect of GHRM on MSME Performance through Competitive Advantage as a mediating variable in culinary MSMEs in Bogor City. The study employed a quantitative approach using a survey method involving 100 culinary MSME owners in Bogor City. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using SPSS version 27 with validity testing, reliability testing, classical assumption testing, simple linear regression analysis, multiple linear regression analysis, coefficient of determination (R²), and path analysis. The results indicate that Green Human Resource Management has a positive and significant effect on Competitive Advantage, Competitive Advantage has a positive and significant effect on MSME Performance, and Green Human Resource Management has a positive and significant effect on MSME Performance both directly and indirectly through Competitive Advantage. Furthermore, Green Human Resource Management has a positive and significant effect on MSME Performance both directly and indirectly through Competitive Advantage. The findings indicate that Competitive Advantage plays an important mediating role in strengthening the relationship between GHRM and MSME Performance. These findings suggest that the implementation of environmentally oriented human resource management practices can improve the competitiveness and business performance of culinary MSMEs in Bogor City.
